newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: New safety rules cut shipowner costs - IMO.
newsitem.headline: New safety rules cut shipowner costs - IMO.

text.p: Shipping companies can cut costs by complying with new safety management rules because they boost efficiency and cut insurance claims, Otto Dijxhoorn of the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) said on Monday.

Speaking in a series of worldwide seminars organised by the IMO, Dijxhoorn stressed the benefits of complying with the International Management Code for Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention (International Management Code or ISM).

"Many shipowners, including some who were opposed to the Code when it was first proposed, now say that implementing it in their organisations was one of the best decisions they had ever made, because the code is not only concerned with safety and environmental protection but with efficiency and cutting costs," he said.

The ISM Code aims to ensure safety at sea and avoid damage to the environment by requiring ships officers and managers vessels to develop, implement and assess pollution prevention management, according to a set of specific guidelines.

It becomes mandatory for passenger ships, bulk carriers, tankers and high speed craft registered to the more than 130 countries which have ratified the 1974 International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) to seek accreditation by July 1, 1998.
The code will be extended to other types of vessels and mobile offshore drilling units by July 1, 2002.

"According to the Norwegian classification society det Norske Veritas (DVN), accidents on board ships cost the industry around $10 billion a year, so obviously there is considerable scope for savings," Dijxhoorn said.

He said that according to the DNV, companies can save five to 10 percent of total costs as the introduction of a safety management system -- one of the key components of the ISM Code -- can result in personal injury pay-outs falling as much as 70 percent and in a fall in repair costs.

Compared to DNV's start up costs of implementing the ISM at $300,000-$600,000 and running costs of $25,000 a year, the company can save around $200,000 a year, making accreditation less of a burden and more of a commercial investment, he said.

He also said that one Swedish insurance company offered a discount last year to those who complied with the Code "because experience has shown that after going through the process, efficiency improved and claims went down".
